# reqwest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/reqwest/^0.13/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#reqwest)reqwest

The `reqwest` crate provides a convenient, higher-level HTTP
[ Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html).

It handles many of the things that most people just expect an HTTP client to do for them.

- Async and [blocking](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)Clients
- Plain bodies, [JSON](https://docs.rs#json),[urlencoded](https://docs.rs#forms),[multipart](https://docs.rs/multipart/index.html)
- Customizable [redirect policy](https://docs.rs#redirect-policies)
- HTTP [Proxies](https://docs.rs#proxies)
- Uses [TLS](https://docs.rs#tls)by default
- Cookies

The [ reqwest::Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html) is asynchronous (requiring Tokio). For
applications wishing  to only make a few HTTP requests, the

[API may be more convenient.](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)

`reqwest::blocking`Additional learning resources include:

[§](https://docs.rs#commercial-support)Commercial Support

For private advice, support, reviews, access to the maintainer, and the
like, reach out for [commercial support](https://seanmonstar.com/sponsor).

[§](https://docs.rs#making-a-get-request)Making a GET request

For a single request, you can use the [ get](https://docs.rs/fn.get.html) shortcut method.

```
let body = reqwest::get("https://www.rust-lang.org")
    .await?
    .text()
    .await?;
println!("body = {body:?}");
```
**NOTE**: If you plan to perform multiple requests, it is best to create a
[ Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html) and reuse it, taking advantage of keep-alive connection
pooling.

[§](https://docs.rs#making-post-requests-or-setting-request-bodies)Making POST requests (or setting request bodies)

There are several ways you can set the body of a request. The basic one is
by using the `body()` method of a [ RequestBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.RequestBuilder.html). This lets you set the
exact raw bytes of what the body should be. It accepts various types,
including

`String` and `Vec<u8>`. If you wish to pass a custom
type, you can use the `reqwest::Body` constructors.```
let client = reqwest::Client::new();
let res = client.post("http://httpbin.org/post")
    .body("the exact body that is sent")
    .send()
    .await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#forms)Forms

It’s very common to want to send form data in a request body. This can be done with any type that can be serialized into form data.

This can be an array of tuples, or a `HashMap`, or a custom type that
implements [ Serialize](http://serde.rs).

The feature `form` is required.

```
// This will POST a body of `foo=bar&baz=quux`
let params = [("foo", "bar"), ("baz", "quux")];
let client = reqwest::Client::new();
let res = client.post("http://httpbin.org/post")
    .form(¶ms)
    .send()
    .await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#json)JSON

There is also a `json` method helper on the [ RequestBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.RequestBuilder.html) that works in
a similar fashion the

`form` method. It can take any value that can be
serialized into JSON.The feature `json` is required.

```
// This will POST a body of `{"lang":"rust","body":"json"}`
let mut map = HashMap::new();
map.insert("lang", "rust");
map.insert("body", "json");
let client = reqwest::Client::new();
let res = client.post("http://httpbin.org/post")
    .json(&map)
    .send()
    .await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#redirect-policies)Redirect Policies

By default, a `Client` will automatically handle HTTP redirects, having a
maximum redirect chain of 10 hops. To customize this behavior, a
[ redirect::Policy](https://docs.rs/redirect/index.html) can be used with a

`ClientBuilder`.[§](https://docs.rs#cookies)Cookies

The automatic storing and sending of session cookies can be enabled with
the [ cookie_store](https://docs.rs/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.cookie_store) method on

`ClientBuilder`.[§](https://docs.rs#proxies)Proxies

**NOTE**: System proxies are enabled by default.

System proxies look in environment variables to set HTTP or HTTPS proxies.

`HTTP_PROXY` or `http_proxy` provide HTTP proxies for HTTP connections while
`HTTPS_PROXY` or `https_proxy` provide HTTPS proxies for HTTPS connections.
`ALL_PROXY` or `all_proxy` provide proxies for both HTTP and HTTPS connections.
If both the all proxy and HTTP or HTTPS proxy variables are set the more specific
HTTP or HTTPS proxies take precedence.

These can be overwritten by adding a [ Proxy](https://docs.rs/struct.Proxy.html) to

`ClientBuilder`
i.e. `let proxy = reqwest::Proxy::http("https://secure.example")?;`
or disabled by calling `ClientBuilder::no_proxy()`.`socks` feature is required if you have configured socks proxy like this:

`export https_proxy=socks5://127.0.0.1:1086`[§](https://docs.rs#tls)TLS

A `Client` will use transport layer security (TLS) by default to connect to
HTTPS destinations.

- Additional server certificates can be configured on a `ClientBuilder`with the`Certificate`
- Client certificates can be added to a `ClientBuilder`with the`Identity`
- Various parts of TLS can also be configured or even disabled on the
`ClientBuilder`.

See more details in the [ tls](https://docs.rs/tls/index.html) module.

[§](https://docs.rs#wasm)WASM

The Client implementation automatically switches to the WASM one when the target_arch is wasm32,
the usage is basically the same as the async api. Some of the features are disabled in wasm
: [ tls](https://docs.rs/tls/index.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/cookie/index.html)

`cookie`[, as well as various](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)

`blocking``ClientBuilder` methods such as `timeout()` and `connector_layer()`.TLS and cookies are provided through the browser environment, so reqwest can issue TLS requests with cookies, but has limited configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional Features

The following are a list of [Cargo features](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section) that can be
enabled or disabled:

- **http2**- *(enabled by default)*: Enables HTTP/2 support.
- **default-tls**- *(enabled by default)*: Provides TLS support to connect over HTTPS.
- **rustls**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `rustls`.
- **rustls-no-provider**: Enables TLS provided by- `rustls`without specifying a crypto provider.
- **native-tls**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `native-tls`.
- **native-tls-vendored**: Enables the- `vendored`feature of- `native-tls`.
- **native-tls-no-alpn**: Enables- `native-tls`without its- `alpn`feature.
- **native-tls-vendored-no-alpn**: Enables- `native-tls-vendored`without its- `alpn`feature.
- **blocking**: Provides the- [blocking](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)client API.
- **charset**- *(enabled by default)*: Improved support for decoding text.
- **cookies**: Provides cookie session support.
- **gzip**: Provides response body gzip decompression.
- **brotli**: Provides response body brotli decompression.
- **zstd**: Provides response body zstd decompression.
- **deflate**: Provides response body deflate decompression.
- **query**: Provides query parameter serialization.
- **form**: Provides form data serialization.
- **json**: Provides serialization and deserialization for JSON bodies.
- **multipart**: Provides functionality for multipart forms.
- **stream**: Adds support for- `futures::Stream`.
- **socks**: Provides SOCKS5 proxy support.
- **hickory-dns**: Enables a hickory-dns async resolver instead of default threadpool using- `getaddrinfo`.
- **system-proxy**- *(enabled by default)*: Use Windows and macOS system proxy settings automatically.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable Features

Some feature flags require additional opt-in by the application, by setting
a `reqwest_unstable` flag.

- **http3**- *(unstable)*: Enables support for sending HTTP/3 requests.

These features are unstable, and experimental. Details about them may be changed in patch releases.

You can pass such a flag to the compiler via `.cargo/config`, or
environment variables, such as:

`RUSTFLAGS="--cfg reqwest_unstable" cargo build`[§](https://docs.rs#sponsors)Sponsors

Support this project by becoming a [sponsor](https://seanmonstar.com/sponsor).

# tar - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tar/^0.4.16/

## Expand description

A library for reading and writing TAR archives

This library provides utilities necessary to manage [TAR archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tar_%28computing%29)
abstracted over a reader or writer. Great strides are taken to ensure that
an archive is never required to be fully resident in memory, and all objects
provide largely a streaming interface to read bytes from.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

When unpacking archives ([ Archive::unpack](https://docs.rs/struct.Archive.html#method.unpack),

[), a best-effort is made to prevent writing files outside the destination directory: paths containing](https://docs.rs/struct.Entry.html#method.unpack_in)

`Entry::unpack_in``..` are rejected, and symlink targets within
the archive are validated before use.**Concurrent mutation of the destination tree is outside the threat model.**
If another process modifies the destination (for example, by atomically
swapping a symlink) while extraction is in progress, this crate may follow
a path outside the intended destination. Preventing such TOCTOU races
requires OS primitives (e.g. `openat`/`O_PATH` used throughout) that this
crate does not use. When extracting untrusted archives in an environment
where the destination may be concurrently modified, use the [ cap-std](https://docs.rs/cap-std/)
crate and/or OS-level sandboxing.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Archive](https://docs.rs/struct.Archive.html)
- A top-level representation of an archive file.
- [Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html)
- A structure for building archives
- [Entries](https://docs.rs/struct.Entries.html)
- An iterator over the entries of an archive.
- [Entry](https://docs.rs/struct.Entry.html)
- A read-only view into an entry of an archive.
- [Entry](https://docs.rs/struct.EntryWriter.html)- Writer
- A writer for a single entry in a tar archive.
- [GnuExt](https://docs.rs/struct.GnuExtSparseHeader.html)- Sparse - Header
- Representation of the entry found to represent extended GNU sparse files.
- [GnuHeader](https://docs.rs/struct.GnuHeader.html)
- Representation of the header of an entry in an archive
- [GnuSparse](https://docs.rs/struct.GnuSparseHeader.html)- Header
- Description of the header of a sparse entry.
- [Header](https://docs.rs/struct.Header.html)
- Representation of the header of an entry in an archive
- [OldHeader](https://docs.rs/struct.OldHeader.html)
- Representation of the header of an entry in an archive
- [PaxExtension](https://docs.rs/struct.PaxExtension.html)
- A key/value pair corresponding to a pax extension.
- [PaxExtensions](https://docs.rs/struct.PaxExtensions.html)
- An iterator over the pax extensions in an archive entry.
- [Ustar](https://docs.rs/struct.UstarHeader.html)- Header
- Representation of the header of an entry in an archive

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Entry](https://docs.rs/enum.EntryType.html)- Type
- Indicate the type of content described by a header.
- [Header](https://docs.rs/enum.HeaderMode.html)- Mode
- Declares the information that should be included when filling a Header from filesystem metadata.
- [Unpacked](https://docs.rs/enum.Unpacked.html)
- When unpacking items the unpacked thing is returned to allow custom additional handling by users. Today the File is returned, in future the enum may be extended with kinds for links, directories etc.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DETERMINISTIC_](https://docs.rs/constant.DETERMINISTIC_TIMESTAMP.html)- TIMESTAMP
- A deterministic, arbitrary, non-zero timestamp that use used as `mtime`of headers when`HeaderMode::Deterministic`

# walkdir - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/walkdir/^2.3.2/

## Expand description

Crate `walkdir` provides an efficient and cross platform implementation
of recursive directory traversal. Several options are exposed to control
iteration, such as whether to follow symbolic links (default off), limit the
maximum number of simultaneous open file descriptors and the ability to
efficiently skip descending into directories.

To use this crate, add `walkdir` as a dependency to your project’s
`Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
walkdir = "2"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#from-the-top)From the top

The [ WalkDir](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html) type builds iterators. The

[type describes values yielded by the iterator. Finally, the](https://docs.rs/struct.DirEntry.html)

`DirEntry`[type is a small wrapper around](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)

`Error`[with additional information, such as if a loop was detected while following symbolic links (not enabled by default).](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/struct.Error.html)

`std::io::Error`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following code recursively iterates over the directory given and prints the path for each entry:

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo") {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
Or, if you’d like to iterate over all entries and ignore any errors that
may arise, use [ filter_map](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/iter/trait.Iterator.html#method.filter_map). (e.g., This code below will silently skip
directories that the owner of the running process does not have permission to
access.)

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").into_iter().filter_map(|e| e.ok()) {
    println!("{}", entry.path().display());
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-follow-symbolic-links)Example: follow symbolic links

The same code as above, except [ follow_links](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html#method.follow_links) is enabled:

```
use walkdir::WalkDir;
for entry in WalkDir::new("foo").follow_links(true) {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-skip-hidden-files-and-directories-on-unix)Example: skip hidden files and directories on unix

This uses the [ filter_entry](https://docs.rs/struct.IntoIter.html#method.filter_entry) iterator adapter to avoid yielding hidden files
and directories efficiently (i.e. without recursing into hidden directories):

```
use walkdir::{DirEntry, WalkDir};
fn is_hidden(entry: &DirEntry) -> bool {
    entry.file_name()
         .to_str()
         .map(|s| s.starts_with("."))
         .unwrap_or(false)
}
let walker = WalkDir::new("foo").into_iter();
for entry in walker.filter_entry(|e| !is_hidden(e)) {
    println!("{}", entry?.path().display());
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [DirEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.DirEntry.html)
- A directory entry.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error produced by recursively walking a directory.
- [Filter](https://docs.rs/struct.FilterEntry.html)- Entry
- A recursive directory iterator that skips entries.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/struct.IntoIter.html)- Iter
- An iterator for recursively descending into a directory.
- [WalkDir](https://docs.rs/struct.WalkDir.html)
- A builder to create an iterator for recursively walking a directory.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [DirEntry](https://docs.rs/trait.DirEntryExt.html)- Ext
- Unix-specific extension methods for `walkdir::DirEntry`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A result type for walkdir operations.

---

# syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/syn/2.0.118/target-redirect/syn/

## Expand description

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user’s code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-a-derive-macro)Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user’s code,
the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
user’s crate.

```
[dependencies]
syn = "2.0"
quote = "1.0"
[lib]
proc-macro = true
```
```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
    let expanded = quote! {
        // ...
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
The [ heapsize](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation
of a derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an
estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
pub trait HeapSize {
    /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
    fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
}
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
structures in their program.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
    a: Box<T>,
    b: u8,
    c: &'a str,
    d: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spans-and-error-reporting)Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler’s error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Broken {
    ok: String,
    bad: std::thread::Thread,
}
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-custom-syntax)Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
using Syn’s parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static! {
    static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
}
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
to be.

[§](https://docs.rs#debugging)Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust’s new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `parsing`
- A stably addressed token buffer supporting efficient traversal based on a cheaply copyable cursor.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Extension traits to provide parsing methods on foreign types.
- [fold](https://docs.rs/fold/index.html)- `fold`
- Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)- `parsing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Facility for interpreting structured content inside of an `Attribute`.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)- `parsing`
- Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A punctuated sequence of syntax tree nodes separated by punctuation.
- [spanned](https://docs.rs/spanned/index.html)- `parsing`and- `printing`
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.
- [visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html)- `visit`
- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
- [visit_](https://docs.rs/visit_mut/index.html)- mut - `visit-mut`
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Token](https://docs.rs/macro.Token.html)
- A type-macro that expands to the name of the Rust type representation of a given token.
- [braced](https://docs.rs/macro.braced.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of curly braces and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [bracketed](https://docs.rs/macro.bracketed.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of square brackets and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_keyword.html)- keyword
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a given identifier as if it were a keyword.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_punctuation.html)- punctuation
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a multi-character symbol as if it were a punctuation token.
- [parenthesized](https://docs.rs/macro.parenthesized.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of parentheses and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_macro_input.html)- macro_ - input - `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote.html)- quote - `parsing`and- `printing`
- Quasi-quotation macro that accepts input like the `quote!`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote_spanned.html)- quote_ - spanned - `parsing`and- `printing`
- This macro is `parse_quote!``quote_spanned!`

- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemTrait.html)- Trait - `full`
- A trait definition: `pub trait Iterator { ... }`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemTraitAlias.html)- Trait - Alias - `full`
- A trait alias: `pub trait SharableIterator = Iterator + Sync`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemType.html)- Type - `full`
- A type alias: `type Result<T> = core::result::Result<T, MyError>`.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemUnion.html)- Union - `full`
- A union definition: `union Foo<A, B> { x: A, y: B }`.
- [ItemUse](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemUse.html)- `full`
- A use declaration: `use alloc::collections::HashMap`.
- [Label](https://docs.rs/struct.Label.html)- `full`
- A lifetime labeling a `for`,`while`, or`loop`.
- [Lifetime](https://docs.rs/struct.Lifetime.html)
- A Rust lifetime: `'a`.
- [Lifetime](https://docs.rs/struct.LifetimeParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A lifetime definition: `'a: 'b + 'c + 'd`.
- [LitBool](https://docs.rs/struct.LitBool.html)
- A boolean literal: `true`or`false`.
- [LitByte](https://docs.rs/struct.LitByte.html)
- A byte literal: `b'f'`.
- [LitByte](https://docs.rs/struct.LitByteStr.html)- Str
- A byte string literal: `b"foo"`.
- [LitCStr](https://docs.rs/struct.LitCStr.html)
- A nul-terminated C-string literal: `c"foo"`.
- [LitChar](https://docs.rs/struct.LitChar.html)
- A character literal: `'a'`.
- [LitFloat](https://docs.rs/struct.LitFloat.html)
- A floating point literal: `1f64`or`1.0e10f64`.
- [LitInt](https://docs.rs/struct.LitInt.html)
- An integer literal: `1`or`1u16`.
- [LitStr](https://docs.rs/struct.LitStr.html)
- A UTF-8 string literal: `"foo"`.
- [Local](https://docs.rs/struct.Local.html)- `full`
- A local `let`binding:`let x: u64 = s.parse()?;`.
- [Local](https://docs.rs/struct.LocalInit.html)- Init - `full`
- The expression assigned in a local `let`binding, including optional diverging`else`block.
- [Macro](https://docs.rs/struct.Macro.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A macro invocation: `println!("{}", mac)`.
- [Meta](https://docs.rs/struct.MetaList.html)- List - `derive`or- `full`
- A structured list within an attribute, like `derive(Copy, Clone)`.
- [Meta](https://docs.rs/struct.MetaNameValue.html)- Name - Value - `derive`or- `full`
- A name-value pair within an attribute, like `feature = "nightly"`.
- [Parenthesized](https://docs.rs/struct.ParenthesizedGenericArguments.html)- Generic - Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Arguments of a function path segment: the `(A, B) -> C`in`Fn(A,B) -> C`.
- [PatConst](https://docs.rs/struct.PatConst.html)- `full`
- A const block: `const { ... }`.
- [PatIdent](https://docs.rs/struct.PatIdent.html)- `full`
- A pattern that binds a new variable: `ref mut binding @ SUBPATTERN`.
- [PatLit](https://docs.rs/struct.PatLit.html)- `full`
- A literal in place of an expression: `1`,`"foo"`.
- [PatMacro](https://docs.rs/struct.PatMacro.html)- `full`
- A macro invocation expression: `format!("{}", q)`.
- [PatOr](https://docs.rs/struct.PatOr.html)- `full`
- A pattern that matches any one of a set of cases.
- [PatParen](https://docs.rs/struct.PatParen.html)- `full`
- A parenthesized pattern: `(A | B)`.
- [PatPath](https://docs.rs/struct.PatPath.html)- `full`
- A path like `core::mem::replace`possibly containing generic parameters and a qualified self-type.
- [PatRange](https://docs.rs/struct.PatRange.html)- `full`
- A range expression: `1..2`,`1..`,`..2`,`1..=2`,`..=2`.
- [PatReference](https://docs.rs/struct.PatReference.html)- `full`
- A reference pattern: `&mut var`.
- [PatRest](https://docs.rs/struct.PatRest.html)- `full`
- The dots in a tuple or slice pattern: `[0, 1, ..]`.
- [PatSlice](https://docs.rs/struct.PatSlice.html)- `full`
- A dynamically sized slice pattern: `[a, b, ref i @ .., y, z]`.
- [PatStruct](https://docs.rs/struct.PatStruct.html)- `full`
- A struct or struct variant pattern: `Variant { x, y, .. }`.
- [PatTuple](https://docs.rs/struct.PatTuple.html)- `full`
- A tuple pattern: `(a, b)`.
- [PatTuple](https://docs.rs/struct.PatTupleStruct.html)- Struct - `full`
- A tuple struct or tuple variant pattern: `Variant(x, y, .., z)`.
- [PatType](https://docs.rs/struct.PatType.html)- `full`
- A type ascription pattern: `foo: f64`.
- [PatWild](https://docs.rs/struct.PatWild.html)- `full`
- A pattern that matches any value: `_`.
- [Path](https://docs.rs/struct.Path.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A path at which a named item is exported (e.g. `alloc::collections::HashMap`).
- [Path](https://docs.rs/struct.PathSegment.html)- Segment - `derive`or- `full`
- A segment of a path together with any path arguments on that segment.
- [Precise](https://docs.rs/struct.PreciseCapture.html)- Capture - `full`
- Precise capturing bound: the ‘use<…>’ in `impl Trait + use<'a, T>`.
- [Predicate](https://docs.rs/struct.PredicateLifetime.html)- Lifetime - `derive`or- `full`
- A lifetime predicate in a `where`clause:`'a: 'b + 'c`.
- [Predicate](https://docs.rs/struct.PredicateType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- A type predicate in a `where`clause:`for<'c> Foo<'c>: Trait<'c>`.
- [QSelf](https://docs.rs/struct.QSelf.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The explicit Self type in a qualified path: the `T`in`<T as Display>::fmt`.
- [Receiver](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)- `full`
- The `self`argument of an associated method.
- [Signature](https://docs.rs/struct.Signature.html)- `full`
- A function signature in a trait or implementation: `unsafe fn initialize(&self)`.
- [Stmt](https://docs.rs/struct.StmtMacro.html)- Macro - `full`
- A macro invocation in statement position.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitBound.html)- Bound - `derive`or- `full`
- A trait used as a bound on a type parameter.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemConst.html)- Item - Const - `full`
- An associated constant within the definition of a trait.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemFn.html)- Item - Fn - `full`
- An associated function within the definition of a trait.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemMacro.html)- Item - Macro - `full`
- A macro invocation within the definition of a trait.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemType.html)- Item - Type - `full`
- An associated type within the definition of a trait.
- [Turbofish](https://docs.rs/struct.Turbofish.html)- `printing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)

- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeArray.html)- Array - `derive`or- `full`

- A parenthesized type equivalent to the inner type.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypePath.html)- Path - `derive`or- `full`

- [TypePtr](https://docs.rs/struct.TypePtr.html)- `derive`or- `full`

- [Static](https://docs.rs/enum.StaticMutability.html)- Mutability - `full`
- The mutability of an `Item::Static`or`ForeignItem::Static`.
- [Stmt](https://docs.rs/enum.Stmt.html)- `full`
- A statement, usually ending in a semicolon.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitBoundModifier.html)- Bound - Modifier - `derive`or- `full`
- A modifier on a trait bound, currently only used for the `?`in`?Sized`.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item declaration within the definition of a trait.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.Type.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The possible types that a Rust value could have.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeParamBound.html)- Param - Bound - `derive`or- `full`
- A trait or lifetime used as a bound on a type parameter.

- A unary operator: `*`,`!`,`-`.

- The visibility level of an item: inherited or `pub`or`pub(restricted)`.
- [Where](https://docs.rs/enum.WherePredicate.html)- Predicate - `derive`or- `full`

# syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2/index.html

## Expand description

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user’s code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-a-derive-macro)Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user’s code,
the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
user’s crate.

```
[dependencies]
syn = "2.0"
quote = "1.0"
[lib]
proc-macro = true
```
```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
    let expanded = quote! {
        // ...
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
The [ heapsize](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation
of a derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an
estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
pub trait HeapSize {
    /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
    fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
}
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
structures in their program.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
    a: Box<T>,
    b: u8,
    c: &'a str,
    d: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spans-and-error-reporting)Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler’s error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Broken {
    ok: String,
    bad: std::thread::Thread,
}
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-custom-syntax)Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
using Syn’s parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static! {
    static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
}
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
to be.

[§](https://docs.rs#debugging)Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust’s new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `parsing`
- A stably addressed token buffer supporting efficient traversal based on a cheaply copyable cursor.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Extension traits to provide parsing methods on foreign types.
- [fold](https://docs.rs/fold/index.html)- `fold`
- Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)- `parsing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Facility for interpreting structured content inside of an `Attribute`.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)- `parsing`
- Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A punctuated sequence of syntax tree nodes separated by punctuation.
- [spanned](https://docs.rs/spanned/index.html)- `parsing`and- `printing`
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.
- [visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html)- `visit`
- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
- [visit_](https://docs.rs/visit_mut/index.html)- mut - `visit-mut`
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Token](https://docs.rs/macro.Token.html)
- A type-macro that expands to the name of the Rust type representation of a given token.
- [braced](https://docs.rs/macro.braced.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of curly braces and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [bracketed](https://docs.rs/macro.bracketed.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of square brackets and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_keyword.html)- keyword
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a given identifier as if it were a keyword.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_punctuation.html)- punctuation
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a multi-character symbol as if it were a punctuation token.
- [parenthesized](https://docs.rs/macro.parenthesized.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of parentheses and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_macro_input.html)- macro_ - input - `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote.html)- quote - `parsing`and- `printing`
- Quasi-quotation macro that accepts input like the `quote!`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote_spanned.html)- quote_ - spanned - `parsing`and- `printing`
- This macro is `parse_quote!``quote_spanned!`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Abi](https://docs.rs/struct.Abi.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The binary interface of a function: `extern "C"`.
- [Angle](https://docs.rs/struct.AngleBracketedGenericArguments.html)- Bracketed - Generic - Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Angle bracketed arguments of a path segment: the `<K, V>`in`HashMap<K, V>`.
- [Arm](https://docs.rs/struct.Arm.html)- `full`
- One arm of a `match`expression:`0..=10 => { return true; }`.
- [Assoc](https://docs.rs/struct.AssocConst.html)- Const - `derive`or- `full`
- An equality constraint on an associated constant: the `PANIC = false`in`Trait<PANIC = false>`.
- [Assoc](https://docs.rs/struct.AssocType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- A binding (equality constraint) on an associated type: the `Item = u8`in`Iterator<Item = u8>`.
- [Attribute](https://docs.rs/struct.Attribute.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- An attribute, like `#[repr(transparent)]`.
- [Bare](https://docs.rs/struct.BareFnArg.html)- FnArg - `derive`or- `full`
- An argument in a function type: the `usize`in`fn(usize) -> bool`.
- [Bare](https://docs.rs/struct.BareVariadic.html)- Variadic - `derive`or- `full`
- The variadic argument of a function pointer like `fn(usize, ...)`.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.Block.html)- `full`
- A braced block containing Rust statements.
- [Bound](https://docs.rs/struct.BoundLifetimes.html)- Lifetimes - `derive`or- `full`
- A set of bound lifetimes: `for<'a, 'b, 'c>`.
- [Const](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A const generic parameter: `const LENGTH: usize`.
- [Constraint](https://docs.rs/struct.Constraint.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- An associated type bound: `Iterator<Item: Display>`.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataEnum.html)- Enum - `derive`
- An enum input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataStruct.html)- Struct - `derive`
- A struct input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataUnion.html)- Union - `derive`
- An untagged union input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Derive](https://docs.rs/struct.DeriveInput.html)- Input - `derive`
- Data structure sent to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error returned when a Syn parser cannot parse the input tokens.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprArray.html)- Array - `full`
- A slice literal expression: `[a, b, c, d]`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAssign.html)- Assign - `full`
- An assignment expression: `a = compute()`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAsync.html)- Async - `full`
- An async block: `async { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAwait.html)- Await - `full`
- An await expression: `fut.await`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBinary.html)- Binary - `derive`or- `full`
- A binary operation: `a + b`,`a += b`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBlock.html)- Block - `full`
- A blocked scope: `{ ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBreak.html)- Break - `full`
- A `break`, with an optional label to break and an optional expression.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprCall.html)- Call - `derive`or- `full`
- A function call expression: `invoke(a, b)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprCast.html)- Cast - `derive`or- `full`
- A cast expression: `foo as f64`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprClosure.html)- Closure - `full`
- A closure expression: `|a, b| a + b`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprConst.html)- Const - `full`
- A const block: `const { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprContinue.html)- Continue - `full`
- A `continue`, with an optional label.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprField.html)- Field - `derive`or- `full`
- Access of a named struct field (`obj.k`) or unnamed tuple struct field (`obj.0`).
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprForLoop.html)- ForLoop - `full`
- A for loop: `for pat in expr { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprGroup.html)- Group - `full`
- An expression contained within invisible delimiters.
- [ExprIf](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprIf.html)- `full`
- An `if`expression with an optional`else`block:`if expr { ... } else { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprIndex.html)- Index - `derive`or- `full`
- A square bracketed indexing expression: `vector[2]`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprInfer.html)- Infer - `full`
- The inferred value of a const generic argument, denoted `_`.
- [ExprLet](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLet.html)- `full`
- A `let`guard:`let Some(x) = opt`.
- [ExprLit](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLit.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A literal in place of an expression: `1`,`"foo"`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLoop.html)- Loop - `full`
- Conditionless loop: `loop { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprMacro.html)- Macro - `derive`or- `full`
- A macro invocation expression: `format!("{}", q)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprMatch.html)- Match - `full`
- A `match`expression:`match n { Some(n) => {}, None => {} }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprMethodCall.html)- Method - Call - `derive`or- `full`
- A method call expression: `x.foo::<T>(a, b)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprParen.html)- Paren - `derive`or- `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprPath.html)- Path - `derive`or- `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprRange.html)- Range - `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprReference.html)- Reference - `derive`or- `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprRepeat.html)- Repeat - `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprReturn.html)- Return - `full`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Attr](https://docs.rs/enum.AttrStyle.html)- Style - `derive`or- `full`
- Distinguishes between attributes that decorate an item and attributes that are contained within an item.
- [BinOp](https://docs.rs/enum.BinOp.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A binary operator: `+`,`+=`,`&`.
- [Captured](https://docs.rs/enum.CapturedParam.html)- Param - `full`
- Single parameter in a precise capturing bound.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/enum.Data.html)- `derive`
- The storage of a struct, enum or union data structure.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A Rust expression.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/enum.FieldMutability.html)- Mutability - `derive`or- `full`
- Unused, but reserved for RFC 3323 restrictions.
- [Fields](https://docs.rs/enum.Fields.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- Data stored within an enum variant or struct.
- [FnArg](https://docs.rs/enum.FnArg.html)- `full`
- An argument in a function signature: the `n: usize`in`fn f(n: usize)`.
- [Foreign](https://docs.rs/enum.ForeignItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item within an `extern`block.
- [Generic](https://docs.rs/enum.GenericArgument.html)- Argument - `derive`or- `full`
- An individual generic argument, like `'a`,`T`, or`Item = T`.
- [Generic](https://docs.rs/enum.GenericParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A generic type parameter, lifetime, or const generic: `T: Into<String>`,`'a: 'b`,`const LEN: usize`.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/enum.ImplItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item within an impl block.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/enum.ImplRestriction.html)- Restriction - `full`
- Unused, but reserved for RFC 3323 restrictions.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/enum.Item.html)- `full`
- Things that can appear directly inside of a module or scope.
- [Lit](https://docs.rs/enum.Lit.html)
- A Rust literal such as a string or integer or boolean.
- [Macro](https://docs.rs/enum.MacroDelimiter.html)- Delimiter - `derive`or- `full`
- A grouping token that surrounds a macro body: `m!(...)`or`m!{...}`or`m![...]`.
- [Member](https://docs.rs/enum.Member.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A struct or tuple struct field accessed in a struct literal or field expression.
- [Meta](https://docs.rs/enum.Meta.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- Content of a compile-time structured attribute.
- [Pat](https://docs.rs/enum.Pat.html)- `full`
- A pattern in a local binding, function signature, match expression, or various other places.
- [Path](https://docs.rs/enum.PathArguments.html)- Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Angle bracketed or parenthesized arguments of a path segment.
- [Pointer](https://docs.rs/enum.PointerMutability.html)- Mutability - `full`
- Mutability of a raw pointer (`*const T`,`*mut T`), in which non-mutable isn’t the implicit default.
- [Range](https://docs.rs/enum.RangeLimits.html)- Limits - `full`
- Limit types of a range, inclusive or exclusive.
- [Return](https://docs.rs/enum.ReturnType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- Return type of a function signature.
- [Static](https://docs.rs/enum.StaticMutability.html)- Mutability - `full`
- The mutability of an `Item::Static`or`ForeignItem::Static`.
- [Stmt](https://docs.rs/enum.Stmt.html)- `full`
- A statement, usually ending in a semicolon.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitBoundModifier.html)- Bound - Modifier - `derive`or- `full`
- A modifier on a trait bound, currently only used for the `?`in`?Sized`.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item declaration within the definition of a trait.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.Type.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The possible types that a Rust value could have.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeParamBound.html)- Param - Bound - `derive`or- `full`
- A trait or lifetime used as a bound on a type parameter.
- [UnOp](https://docs.rs/enum.UnOp.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A unary operator: `*`,`!`,`-`.
- [UseTree](https://docs.rs/enum.UseTree.html)- `full`
- A suffix of an import tree in a `use`item:`Type as Renamed`or`*`.
- [Visibility](https://docs.rs/enum.Visibility.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The visibility level of an item: inherited or `pub`or`pub(restricted)`.
- [Where](https://docs.rs/enum.WherePredicate.html)- Predicate - `derive`or- `full`
- A single predicate in a `where`clause:`T: Deserialize<'de>`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

# File in syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2/struct.File.html

**crate feature**only.

`full`## Expand description

A complete file of Rust source code.

Typically `File` objects are created with [ parse_file](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_file.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Parse a Rust source file into a `syn::File` and print out a debug
representation of the syntax tree.

```
use std::env;
use std::fs;
use std::process;
fn main() {
    let mut args = env::args();
    let _ = args.next(); // executable name
    let filename = match (args.next(), args.next()) {
        (Some(filename), None) => filename,
        _ => {
            eprintln!("Usage: dump-syntax path/to/filename.rs");
            process::exit(1);
        }
    };
    let src = fs::read_to_string(&filename).expect("unable to read file");
    let syntax = syn::parse_file(&src).expect("unable to parse file");
    // Debug impl is available if Syn is built with "extra-traits" feature.
    println!("{:#?}", syntax);
}
```
Running with its own source code as input, this program prints output that begins with:

```
File {
    shebang: None,
    attrs: [],
    items: [
        Use(
            ItemUse {
                attrs: [],
                vis: Inherited,
                use_token: Use,
                leading_colon: None,
                tree: Path(
                    UsePath {
                        ident: Ident(
                            std,
                        ),
                        colon2_token: Colon2,
                        tree: Name(
                            UseName {
                                ident: Ident(
                                    env,
                                ),
                            },
                        ),
                    },
                ),
                semi_token: Semi,
            },
        ),
...
```

`derive` or `full`## Expand description

A Rust expression.

*This type is available only if Syn is built with the  "derive" or "full"
feature, but most of the variants are not available unless “full” is enabled.*

[§](https://docs.rs#syntax-tree-enums)Syntax tree enums

This type is a syntax tree enum. In Syn this and other syntax tree enums are designed to be traversed using the following rebinding idiom.

```
let expr: Expr = /* ... */;
match expr {
    Expr::MethodCall(expr) => {
        /* ... */
    }
    Expr::Cast(expr) => {
        /* ... */
    }
    Expr::If(expr) => {
        /* ... */
    }
    /* ... */
```
We begin with a variable `expr` of type `Expr` that has no fields
(because it is an enum), and by matching on it and rebinding a variable
with the same name `expr` we effectively imbue our variable with all of
the data fields provided by the variant that it turned out to be. So for
example above if we ended up in the `MethodCall` case then we get to use
`expr.receiver`, `expr.args` etc; if we ended up in the `If` case we get
to use `expr.cond`, `expr.then_branch`, `expr.else_branch`.

This approach avoids repeating the variant names twice on every line.

```
// Repetitive; recommend not doing this.
match expr {
    Expr::MethodCall(ExprMethodCall { method, args, .. }) => {
```
In general, the name to which a syntax tree enum variant is bound should be a suitable name for the complete syntax tree enum type.

```
// Binding is called `base` which is the name I would use if I were
// assigning `*discriminant.base` without an `if let`.
if let Expr::Tuple(base) = *discriminant.base {
```
A sign that you may not be choosing the right variable names is if you
see names getting repeated in your code, like accessing
`receiver.receiver` or `pat.pat` or `cond.cond`.

An unspecified invalid expression.

```
use core::mem;
use quote::ToTokens;
use syn::{parse_quote, Expr};
fn unparenthesize(e: &mut Expr) {
    while let Expr::Paren(paren) = e {
        *e = mem::replace(&mut *paren.expr, Expr::PLACEHOLDER);
    }
}
fn main() {
    let mut e: Expr = parse_quote! { ((1 + 1)) };
    unparenthesize(&mut e);
    assert_eq!("1 + 1", e.to_token_stream().to_string());
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/syn/expr.rs.html#830-832)#### pub fn [parse_without_eager_brace](https://docs.rs#method.parse_without_eager_brace)(input: [ParseStream](https://docs.rs/parse/type.ParseStream.html)<'_>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)>

**crate features **`full` and `parsing` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/syn/expr.rs.html#830-832)

#### pub fn [parse_without_eager_brace](https://docs.rs#method.parse_without_eager_brace)(input: [ParseStream](https://docs.rs/parse/type.ParseStream.html)<'_>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)>

**crate features**only.

`full` and `parsing`An alternative to the primary `Expr::parse` parser (from the [ Parse](https://docs.rs/parse/trait.Parse.html)
trait) for ambiguous syntactic positions in which a trailing brace
should not be taken as part of the expression.

Rust grammar has an ambiguity where braces sometimes turn a path
expression into a struct initialization and sometimes do not. In the
following code, the expression `S {}` is one expression. Presumably
there is an empty struct `struct S {}` defined somewhere which it is
instantiating.

```
let _ = *S {};
// parsed by rustc as: `*(S {})`
```
We would want to parse the above using `Expr::parse` after the `=`
token.

But in the following, `S {}` is *not* a struct init expression.

```
if *S {} {}
// parsed by rustc as:
//
//    if (*S) {
//        /* empty block */
//    }
//    {
//        /* another empty block */
//    }
```
For that reason we would want to parse if-conditions using
`Expr::parse_without_eager_brace` after the `if` token. Same for similar
syntactic positions such as the condition expr after a `while` token or
the expr at the top of a `match`.

The Rust grammar’s choices around which way this ambiguity is resolved at various syntactic positions is fairly arbitrary. Really either parse behavior could work in most positions, and language designers just decide each case based on which is more likely to be what the programmer had in mind most of the time.

```
if return S {} {}
// parsed by rustc as:
//
//    if (return (S {})) {
//    }
//
// but could equally well have been this other arbitrary choice:
//
//    if (return S) {
//    }
//    {}
```
Note the grammar ambiguity on trailing braces is distinct from
precedence and is not captured by assigning a precedence level to the
braced struct init expr in relation to other operators. This can be
illustrated by `return 0..S {}` vs `match 0..S {}`. The former parses as
`return (0..(S {}))` implying tighter precedence for struct init than
`..`, while the latter parses as `match (0..S) {}` implying tighter
precedence for `..` than struct init, a contradiction.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/syn/expr.rs.html#892-894)#### pub fn [parse_with_earlier_boundary_rule](https://docs.rs#method.parse_with_earlier_boundary_rule)(input: [ParseStream](https://docs.rs/parse/type.ParseStream.html)<'_>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)>

**crate features **`full` and `parsing` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/syn/expr.rs.html#892-894)

#### pub fn [parse_with_earlier_boundary_rule](https://docs.rs#method.parse_with_earlier_boundary_rule)(input: [ParseStream](https://docs.rs/parse/type.ParseStream.html)<'_>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)>

**crate features**only.

`full` and `parsing`An alternative to the primary `Expr::parse` parser (from the [ Parse](https://docs.rs/parse/trait.Parse.html)
trait) for syntactic positions in which expression boundaries are placed
more eagerly than done by the typical expression grammar. This includes
expressions at the head of a statement or in the right-hand side of a

`match` arm.Compare the following cases:

```
let _ = match result {
    () if guard => if cond { f } else { g }
    () => false,
};
```
```
let _ = || {
    if cond { f } else { g }
    ()
};
```
`let _ = [if cond { f } else { g } ()];`The same sequence of tokens `if cond { f } else { g } ()` appears in
expression position 3 times. The first two syntactic positions use eager
placement of expression boundaries, and parse as `Expr::If`, with the
adjacent `()` becoming `Pat::Tuple` or `Expr::Tuple`. In contrast, the
third case uses standard expression boundaries and parses as
`Expr::Call`.

As with [ parse_without_eager_brace](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html#method.parse_without_eager_brace), this ambiguity in the Rust
grammar is independent of precedence.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/syn/expr.rs.html#908-924)#### pub fn [peek](https://docs.rs#method.peek)(input: [ParseStream](https://docs.rs/parse/type.ParseStream.html)<'_>) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

**crate feature **`parsing` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/syn/expr.rs.html#908-924)

#### pub fn [peek](https://docs.rs#method.peek)(input: [ParseStream](https://docs.rs/parse/type.ParseStream.html)<'_>) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

**crate feature**only.

`parsing`Returns whether the next token in the parse stream is one that might possibly form the beginning of an expr.

This classification is a load-bearing part of the grammar of some Rust
expressions, notably `return` and `break`. For example `return < …` will
never parse `<` as a binary operator regardless of what comes after,
because `<` is a legal starting token for an expression and so it’s
required to be continued as a return value, such as `return <Struct as Trait>::CONST`. Meanwhile `return > …` treats the `>` as a binary
operator because it cannot be a starting token for any Rust expression.

## Expand description

A type-macro that expands to the name of the Rust type representation of a given token.

As a type, `Token!` is commonly used in the type of struct fields, the type
of a `let` statement, or in turbofish for a `parse` function.

```
use syn::{Ident, Token};
use syn::parse::{Parse, ParseStream, Result};
// `struct Foo;`
pub struct UnitStruct {
    struct_token: Token![struct],
    ident: Ident,
    semi_token: Token![;],
}
impl Parse for UnitStruct {
    fn parse(input: ParseStream) -> Result<Self> {
        let struct_token: Token![struct] = input.parse()?;
        let ident: Ident = input.parse()?;
        let semi_token = input.parse::<Token![;]>()?;
        Ok(UnitStruct { struct_token, ident, semi_token })
    }
}
```
As an expression, `Token!` is used for peeking tokens or instantiating
tokens from a span.

```
fn make_unit_struct(name: Ident) -> UnitStruct {
    let span = name.span();
    UnitStruct {
        struct_token: Token![struct](span),
        ident: name,
        semi_token: Token![;](span),
    }
}
if input.peek(Token![struct]) {
    let unit_struct: UnitStruct = input.parse()?;
    /* ... */
}
```
See the [token module](https://docs.rs/token/index.html) documentation for details and examples.

# braced in syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2/macro.braced.html

```
macro_rules! braced {
    ($content:ident in $cursor:expr) => { ... };
}
```
Available on

**crate feature**only.`parsing`## Expand description

Parse a set of curly braces and expose their content to subsequent parsers.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use syn::{braced, token, Ident, Result, Token, Type};
use syn::parse::{Parse, ParseStream};
use syn::punctuated::Punctuated;
// Parse a simplified struct syntax like:
//
//     struct S {
//         a: A,
//         b: B,
//     }
struct Struct {
    struct_token: Token![struct],
    ident: Ident,
    brace_token: token::Brace,
    fields: Punctuated<Field, Token![,]>,
}
struct Field {
    name: Ident,
    colon_token: Token![:],
    ty: Type,
}
impl Parse for Struct {
    fn parse(input: ParseStream) -> Result<Self> {
        let content;
        Ok(Struct {
            struct_token: input.parse()?,
            ident: input.parse()?,
            brace_token: braced!(content in input),
            fields: content.parse_terminated(Field::parse, Token![,])?,
        })
    }
}
impl Parse for Field {
    fn parse(input: ParseStream) -> Result<Self> {
        Ok(Field {
            name: input.parse()?,
            colon_token: input.parse()?,
            ty: input.parse()?,
        })
    }
}
```

# bracketed in syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2/macro.bracketed.html

```
macro_rules! bracketed {
    ($content:ident in $cursor:expr) => { ... };
}
```
Available on

**crate feature**only.`parsing`## Expand description

Parse a set of square brackets and expose their content to subsequent parsers.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use proc_macro2::TokenStream;
use syn::{bracketed, token, Result, Token};
use syn::parse::{Parse, ParseStream};
// Parse an outer attribute like:
//
//     #[repr(C, packed)]
struct OuterAttribute {
    pound_token: Token![#],
    bracket_token: token::Bracket,
    content: TokenStream,
}
impl Parse for OuterAttribute {
    fn parse(input: ParseStream) -> Result<Self> {
        let content;
        Ok(OuterAttribute {
            pound_token: input.parse()?,
            bracket_token: bracketed!(content in input),
            content: content.parse()?,
        })
    }
}
```

# custom_keyword in syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2/macro.custom_keyword.html

```
macro_rules! custom_keyword {
    ($ident:ident) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Define a type that supports parsing and printing a given identifier as if it were a keyword.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

As a convention, it is recommended that this macro be invoked within a
module called `kw` or `keyword` and that the resulting parser be invoked
with a `kw::` or `keyword::` prefix.

```
mod kw {
    syn::custom_keyword!(whatever);
}
```
The generated syntax tree node supports the following operations just like any built-in keyword token.

-
[Peeking](https://docs.rs/parse/struct.ParseBuffer.html#method.peek)—`input.peek(kw::whatever)`
-
[Parsing](https://docs.rs/parse/struct.ParseBuffer.html#method.parse)—`input.parse::<kw::whatever>()?`
-
[Printing](https://docs.rs/quote/1.0.45/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/quote/to_tokens/trait.ToTokens.html)—`quote!( ... #whatever_token ... )`
-
Construction from a `Span``let whatever_token = kw::whatever(sp)`
-
Field access to its span — `let sp = whatever_token.span`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This example parses input that looks like `bool = true` or `str = "value"`.
The key must be either the identifier `bool` or the identifier `str`. If
`bool`, the value may be either `true` or `false`. If `str`, the value may
be any string literal.

The symbols `bool` and `str` are not reserved keywords in Rust so these are
not considered keywords in the `syn::token` module. Like any other
identifier that is not a keyword, these can be declared as custom keywords
by crates that need to use them as such.

```
use syn::{LitBool, LitStr, Result, Token};
use syn::parse::{Parse, ParseStream};
mod kw {
    syn::custom_keyword!(bool);
    syn::custom_keyword!(str);
}
enum Argument {
    Bool {
        bool_token: kw::bool,
        eq_token: Token![=],
        value: LitBool,
    },
    Str {
        str_token: kw::str,
        eq_token: Token![=],
        value: LitStr,
    },
}
impl Parse for Argument {
    fn parse(input: ParseStream) -> Result<Self> {
        let lookahead = input.lookahead1();
        if lookahead.peek(kw::bool) {
            Ok(Argument::Bool {
                bool_token: input.parse::<kw::bool>()?,
                eq_token: input.parse()?,
                value: input.parse()?,
            })
        } else if lookahead.peek(kw::str) {
            Ok(Argument::Str {
                str_token: input.parse::<kw::str>()?,
                eq_token: input.parse()?,
                value: input.parse()?,
            })
        } else {
            Err(lookahead.error())
        }
    }
}
```

---

# custom_punctuation in syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2/macro.custom_punctuation.html

```
macro_rules! custom_punctuation {
    ($ident:ident, $($tt:tt)+) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Define a type that supports parsing and printing a multi-character symbol as if it were a punctuation token.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

`syn::custom_punctuation!(LeftRightArrow, <=>);`The generated syntax tree node supports the following operations just like any built-in punctuation token.

-
[Peeking](https://docs.rs/parse/struct.ParseBuffer.html#method.peek)—`input.peek(LeftRightArrow)`
-
[Parsing](https://docs.rs/parse/struct.ParseBuffer.html#method.parse)—`input.parse::<LeftRightArrow>()?`
-
[Printing](https://docs.rs/quote/1.0.45/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/quote/to_tokens/trait.ToTokens.html)—`quote!( ... #lrarrow ... )`
-
Construction from a `Span``let lrarrow = LeftRightArrow(sp)`
-
Construction from multiple `Span``let lrarrow = LeftRightArrow([sp, sp, sp])`
-
Field access to its spans — `let spans = lrarrow.spans`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use core::iter;
use proc_macro2::{TokenStream, TokenTree};
use syn::parse::{Parse, ParseStream, Peek, Result};
use syn::punctuated::Punctuated;
use syn::Expr;
syn::custom_punctuation!(PathSeparator, </>);
// expr </> expr </> expr ...
struct PathSegments {
    segments: Punctuated<Expr, PathSeparator>,
}
impl Parse for PathSegments {
    fn parse(input: ParseStream) -> Result<Self> {
        let mut segments = Punctuated::new();
        let first = parse_until(input, PathSeparator)?;
        segments.push_value(syn::parse2(first)?);
        while input.peek(PathSeparator) {
            segments.push_punct(input.parse()?);
            let next = parse_until(input, PathSeparator)?;
            segments.push_value(syn::parse2(next)?);
        }
        Ok(PathSegments { segments })
    }
}
fn parse_until<E: Peek>(input: ParseStream, end: E) -> Result<TokenStream> {
    let mut tokens = TokenStream::new();
    while !input.is_empty() && !input.peek(end) {
        let next: TokenTree = input.parse()?;
        tokens.extend(iter::once(next));
    }
    Ok(tokens)
}
fn main() {
    let input = r#" a::b </> c::d::e "#;
    let _: PathSegments = syn::parse_str(input).unwrap();
}
```

# parenthesized in syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2/macro.parenthesized.html

```
macro_rules! parenthesized {
    ($content:ident in $cursor:expr) => { ... };
}
```
Available on

**crate feature**only.`parsing`## Expand description

Parse a set of parentheses and expose their content to subsequent parsers.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use syn::{parenthesized, token, Ident, Result, Token, Type};
use syn::parse::{Parse, ParseStream};
use syn::punctuated::Punctuated;
// Parse a simplified tuple struct syntax like:
//
//     struct S(A, B);
struct TupleStruct {
    struct_token: Token![struct],
    ident: Ident,
    paren_token: token::Paren,
    fields: Punctuated<Type, Token![,]>,
    semi_token: Token![;],
}
impl Parse for TupleStruct {
    fn parse(input: ParseStream) -> Result<Self> {
        let content;
        Ok(TupleStruct {
            struct_token: input.parse()?,
            ident: input.parse()?,
            paren_token: parenthesized!(content in input),
            fields: content.parse_terminated(Type::parse, Token![,])?,
            semi_token: input.parse()?,
        })
    }
}
```

# parse_macro_input in syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2/macro.parse_macro_input.html

```
macro_rules! parse_macro_input {
    ($tokenstream:ident as $ty:ty) => { ... };
    ($tokenstream:ident with $parser:path) => { ... };
    ($tokenstream:ident) => { ... };
}
```
**crate features**only.

`parsing` and `proc-macro`## Expand description

Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.

Refer to the [ parse module](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html) documentation for more details about parsing
in Syn.

[§](https://docs.rs#intended-usage)Intended usage

This macro must be called from a function that returns
`proc_macro::TokenStream`. Usually this will be your proc macro entry point,
the function that has the #[proc_macro] / #[proc_macro_derive] /
#[proc_macro_attribute] attribute.

```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, Result};
use syn::parse::{Parse, ParseStream};
struct MyMacroInput {
    /* ... */
}
impl Parse for MyMacroInput {
    fn parse(input: ParseStream) -> Result<Self> {
        /* ... */
    }
}
#[proc_macro]
pub fn my_macro(tokens: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    let input = parse_macro_input!(tokens as MyMacroInput);
    /* ... */
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#usage-with-parser)Usage with Parser

This macro can also be used with the [ Parser trait](https://docs.rs/parse/trait.Parser.html) for types that have
multiple ways that they can be parsed.

```
impl MyMacroInput {
    fn parse_alternate(input: ParseStream) -> Result<Self> {
        /* ... */
    }
}
#[proc_macro]
pub fn my_macro(tokens: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    let input = parse_macro_input!(tokens with MyMacroInput::parse_alternate);
    /* ... */
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#expansion)Expansion

`parse_macro_input!($variable as $Type)` expands to something like:

```
match syn::parse::<$Type>($variable) {
    Ok(syntax_tree) => syntax_tree,
    Err(err) => return proc_macro::TokenStream::from(err.to_compile_error()),
}
```

# parse_quote in syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2/macro.parse_quote.html

```
macro_rules! parse_quote {
    ($($tt:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
**crate features**only.

`parsing` and `printing`## Expand description

Quasi-quotation macro that accepts input like the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/quote/1.0/quote/index.html) macro but uses
type inference to figure out a return type for those tokens.

The return type can be any syntax tree node that implements the [ Parse](https://docs.rs/parse/trait.Parse.html)
trait.

```
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_quote, Stmt};
fn main() {
    let name = quote!(v);
    let ty = quote!(u8);
    let stmt: Stmt = parse_quote! {
        let #name: #ty = Default::default();
    };
    println!("{:#?}", stmt);
}
```
*This macro is available only if Syn is built with both the  "parsing" and
"printing" features.*

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following helper function adds a bound `T: HeapSize` to every type
parameter `T` in the input generics.

```
use syn::{parse_quote, Generics, GenericParam};
// Add a bound `T: HeapSize` to every type parameter T.
fn add_trait_bounds(mut generics: Generics) -> Generics {
    for param in &mut generics.params {
        if let GenericParam::Type(type_param) = param {
            type_param.bounds.push(parse_quote!(HeapSize));
        }
    }
    generics
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#special-cases)Special cases

This macro can parse the following additional types as a special case even
though they do not implement the `Parse` trait.

- `Attribute`- `#[...]`or inner like- `#![...]`
- `Vec<Attribute>`
- `Punctuated<T, P>`- `T`separated by punctuation- `P`with optional trailing punctuation
- `Vec<Arm>`- `match`expression
- `Vec<Stmt>`- `Block::parse_within`
- `Pat`- `Box<Pat>`- `Pat::parse_multi_with_leading_vert`
- `Field`

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the tokens fail to parse as the expected syntax tree type. The caller is responsible for ensuring that the input tokens are syntactically valid.

---

# quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/1.0/quote/index.html

## Expand description

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller’s crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text
editor or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor’s brace matching,
syntax highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than
compiling that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass
it around, mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens
to compile into the macro caller’s crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[dependencies]
quote = "1.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following quasi-quoted block of code is something you might find in [a](https://serde.rs/)
procedural macro having to do with data structure serialization. The `#var`
syntax performs interpolation of runtime variables into the quoted tokens.
Check out the documentation of the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for more detail about
the syntax. See also the

[macro which is important for implementing hygienic procedural macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)

`quote_spanned!````
let tokens = quote! {
    struct SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        value: &'a #field_ty,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<#item_ty>,
    }
    impl #generics serde::Serialize for SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
        where
            S: serde::Serializer,
        {
            #path(self.value, serializer)
        }
    }
    SerializeWith {
        value: #value,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData::<#item_ty>,
    }
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-macro-code-generators)Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through
[prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease) before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated
code it is convenient for a human to read and debug.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [format_](https://docs.rs/macro.format_ident.html)- ident
- Formatting macro for constructing `Ident`s.
- [quote](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html)
- The whole point.
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)- spanned
- Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within the macro invocation.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Ident](https://docs.rs/trait.IdentFragment.html)- Fragment
- Specialized formatting trait used by `format_ident!`.
- [ToTokens](https://docs.rs/trait.ToTokens.html)
- Types that can be interpolated inside a `quote!`invocation.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/trait.TokenStreamExt.html)- Stream - Ext
- TokenStream extension trait with methods for appending tokens.
